content.p: In the spring of 1824 an Egyptian fleet carrying Albanian soldiers sailed against Kasos, a dry island of about twelve miles in length whose ships had raided Ottoman and Egyptian coasts for years and made it one of the most exposed naval bases of the Greek revolt. In a matter of days the island fell. Its fighting men were killed or driven into the hills, thousands of women and children were taken to the slave markets, and its ships were confiscated. Greeks remember the event as the Holocaust of Kasos. Historians do not agree on how many died, and even the date of the landing is given differently from one account to the next.

The attack was part of a wider Ottoman effort that year to break the island fleets. Kasos and Psara were hit within weeks of each other, and the Egyptian operation also cleared the way for the later landing of Egyptian troops in the Peloponnese.

By the account of the historian George Finlay, Kasos had about seven thousand inhabitants. It had no secure harbour and an iron-bound coast, yet it owned fifteen square-rigged vessels and some forty smaller craft. According to Finlay, for three years those ships had raided Crete, Rhodes and Cyprus and the coasts of Anatolia, Syria and Egypt. He added that the Kasiots were said to have killed their prisoners at sea, noting that few Turkish captives were ever brought ashore, and he thought the accusation probably well founded. He also observed that mercy was as little practised by the Christian side as by the Muslim one in the early years of the revolution.

Greek accounts stress a different side of that record. According to the account published on Anamniseis, a Kasiot ship brought home the news of the uprising on 23 April 1821, and the island at once put its fleet at the disposal of the struggle. Kasiot vessels bombarded the fortress of Rhodes in May of that year. The main body of the fleet went to Crete, where the rebels were fighting forces sent by Mehmed Ali, and carried food, arms and Cretan refugees. A Greek historical summary on zougla.gr says the Kasiots also seized ships, Turkish or European, that were carrying food and munitions to Ottoman forces on Crete. Anamniseis adds a daring raid on the Egyptian port of Damietta, led by Captain Hatzi-Nikolas Makris with four ships, in which, it says, fifteen food-laden vessels were captured. The food went to a starving Kasos, and the ships were handed to the revolutionary government to be turned into fireships.

That activity made Kasos a target. Finlay wrote that Sultan Mahmud selected Psara and Kasos as the first objects of attack because they were the most exposed naval bases of the Greeks, and described Kasos as "an eyesore and a torment to Syria and Egypt". The plan, he said, was for the sultan and Mehmed Ali to strike both islands suddenly and at the same time with two fleets.

Once the Egyptians had crushed the last rebel centres on Crete, Kasos was the next obvious step. Many armed Cretans, among them men under Dimitrios Kourmoulis and Astrinos Hatzidakis, had taken refuge on the island, according to the zougla.gr account.

That account says word of Egyptian intentions had reached the island by mid-April 1824. On 12 May the island's notables wrote to the revolutionary government asking for help and got no reply. Two days later the Egyptian fleet appeared offshore, coming from its base at Souda in Crete. The Kasiots asked again on 17 May. The answer, that there was no money, arrived on 27 May, the day the fleet came back. Anamniseis tells the same story from another angle: Hydra's own money from a loan had not arrived, and the private means of the three sea-faring islands could not cover even their own needs, so Kasos stood alone.

The islanders prepared as well as they could. Anamniseis says they hauled their ships ashore and raised earthworks along the northern side of the island, from Agia Marina to Emporio, mounting the ships' guns and arming everyone who could hold a weapon, boys and old men included. Early in May, that account continues, the fleet blockaded the island and shelled it, and boat landings were beaten off, so that for days the sea washed up bodies of Egyptian and Albanian crewmen. Then, it says, the frigate of Ismael Gibraltar struck a reef and had to be taken to Rhodes for repair, and the fleet left. A few days later it returned reinforced by 35 more ships.

Sources agree on the broad outline and differ on the details. Finlay says the Egyptian force consisted of three frigates and ten sloops under Ismael Gibraltar Pasha, carrying three thousand Albanians under Hussein Bey Djeritlee. The zougla.gr history gives the fleet as between 25 and 45 ships depending on the source, with three to four thousand Albanian soldiers, and calls Ismael Gibraltar an Algerian admiral. A Greek City Times report on a 2021 anniversary speech gives the figure of 45 ships.

The dates differ. The ime.gr chronology puts the landing at the end of May 1824. The zougla.gr account and Anamniseis place the opening bombardment on 27 May; zougla.gr puts the decisive landing in the night of 28 to 29 May, and Anamniseis in the night of 29 May. ERT, the Greek state broadcaster, marks 7 June as the day of the destruction, and Finlay, writing in the nineteenth century, says the Albanians landed at night on 19 June. This account follows the Greek sources for the sequence and notes where Finlay differs.

According to zougla.gr, Hussein staged a diversionary landing on the shore north of Agia Marina, where the Kasiots concentrated their attention. Meanwhile thirty boats packed with Albanians under a commander named Mousa put men ashore without opposition at a steep spot called Antiperatos. A second wave followed and by dawn about 2,000 Albanian soldiers were behind the defenders. Anamniseis gives a smaller first party, 200 men, who killed five of the six guards at the spot; one guard escaped to give the alarm. It also says Mousa was helped by a man named Zacharias, whom it calls a traitor; only Anamniseis makes this claim and it gives no source for it. Finlay, writing of the landing as he understood it, said the islanders lived in four villages high on the mountain and that the surprise was complete.

The Kasiots found themselves between two fires. Zougla.gr says Hussein called on them to surrender in return for their lives and they refused. Anamniseis says the defenders, under Ioannis Grigoriadis and Markos Malliarakis, fell back to the village of Agia Marina, where a fierce, unequal battle was fought, and then withdrew to the mountains, leaving 100 dead behind. The villages passed into the hands of the attackers.

One episode stands out in the accounts of the fall. Captain Markos Ioannou, called Malliarakis or Diakomarkos, held out in the mountains with about forty men, according to zougla.gr. Anamniseis says he fought for four hours against 2,000 Albanians and inflicted heavy losses before he was captured alive.

The two accounts then differ over the reason he was still alive. Zougla.gr says Hussein, impressed by his courage, decided to spare him. Anamniseis says he was bound and led before Hussein. In both versions, once he was freed from his bonds, or while he was being taken, he seized a blade from a guard and killed three of them. Zougla.gr says he died soon after. Anamniseis says the other guards threw themselves on him and cut him down.

With the resistance broken came what the Greek accounts call a general slaughter and enslavement. The zougla.gr history says about 2,000 were killed and as many women and children taken to be sold in the slave markets of the East. Anamniseis also speaks of about 2,000 women and children carried to the ships, and says the attackers killed, plundered and took prisoners. The ERT archive page says about 2,000 islanders were slaughtered and as many children and women were seized, later to be sold in the slave markets of Egypt and Crete. At the 2022 commemoration reported by The National Herald, the president of the Kassian Brotherhood of America, Antonis Perselis, put it in these terms, in the paper's English rendering: "It is the day that about 2,000 Kassians lost their lives defending their homeland and hundreds of women and children were sold in the slave markets."

Finlay's figures are different. In his telling the men capable of bearing arms were killed without mercy, as were the old women, and the young women and children judged fit for the slave market of Alexandria were taken to the ships. He writes that five hundred Kasiot seamen were slain and that over two thousand women and children were enslaved. He also says fourteen square-rigged vessels and about thirty small craft were captured, that the Albanians lost only thirty killed and wounded, and that they were allowed twenty-four hours to plunder before Ismael Gibraltar and Hussein restored order and gave protection to every Greek who submitted. The gap between 500 and 2,000 dead is not settled by these sources.

Zougla.gr adds that the Albanian soldiers who were Christians tried in vain to stop the killing of civilians and the abduction of girls, and that the Kasiot ships were confiscated, with many islanders forced to serve in their crews to save their families.

Hussein installed a Turkish governor on Kasos, according to zougla.gr, secured the surrender of neighbouring Karpathos without a fight, and sailed for Souda. The Greek fleet of Hydra and Spetses, alarmed that the Egyptians might turn on them next, sailed for Kasos. Admiral Georgios Sachtouris went ashore on 21 June and found the island wrecked, with few people left, as he wrote in his memoirs; on 24 June he learned of the destruction of Psara from a Santorini ship flying a Russian flag.

The ime.gr chronology notes that the Greek fleet which sailed to Kasos in mid-June was hundreds of miles from Psara when the Ottoman fleet approached it in the last ten days of June. It describes Kasos and Psara as islands where the occupations resulted in extensive massacres, plundering and destruction, and links the failure to help to civil conflict in the Peloponnese that had ended the activity of the revolutionary administration. Finlay was sharper. He wrote that the Albanians of Hydra and Spetses had been slow to help Kasos and Psara, and that fear for their own safety, aroused when the fate of Psara was known, drove them to act too late.

The zougla.gr history notes that putting down the Cretan revolt and destroying Kasos opened the way for the Egyptian landing in the Peloponnese under Ibrahim in February 1825. Finlay adds that Hussein, the conqueror of Kasos, later reached Ibrahim's camp with reinforcements, and that his advice shaped the attack on the island of Sphakteria off Navarin.

Anamniseis, whose author says he found a book on revolutionary movements, with a chapter on the Greek Revolution, in an army camp library while serving in the United States army in 1960, contrasts the fall of Kasos with the massacre at Chios and the exodus from Mesolonghi, which Delacroix painted, and the fall of Psara, which Dionysios Solomos celebrated in verse. The fall of Kasos, it says, was sung in a Kasiot folk song, and Karpathos mourned it with one of its own.

The day is still marked. On 12 June 2022 the Kassian Benevolent Society of America held its 198th commemoration at the Kassian Club in the Bronx, with a moment of silence, recitations of the laments of Karpathos and Kasos, and children in island costume dancing. In June 2021 the Greek state minister Giorgos Gerapetritis spoke on Kasos itself, calling the Kasos holocaust a living monument and, in remarks to ERT, using the anniversary to send a message to Turkey about Greek sovereignty. Greek reports of the 200th anniversary in 2024 used the same name for the event.
